nogpu.about.heading.source: Artificial life, evolving on your GPU

nogpu.about.p1.source: Tidemote is a sealed biosphere of hundreds of thousands to millions of particles, simulated live in the browser with WebGPU. Cells photosynthesize in the tide's moving light, graze, hunt and scavenge, and build their children out of silt. Children mutate into new species, bonded species grow into multicellular bodies, and the climate turns every 10–18 minutes. Leave it running and it keeps changing.

prev.text: Tidemote is a sealed biosphere of up to millions of particles, and all of them live, eat, breed, and die in your browser, simulated on the GPU with WebGPU. Some cells drink the moving light of the tide. Others graze on the photosynthesizers, and others hunt the grazers. Scavengers break down the dead and return them to the water as silt, and from that silt the next generation builds its children. Children mutate into new species. Species that bond grow into bodies: filaments, branched fronds, spirals, packed tissues. Some of these bodies grow beating tails and swim. Every 10 to 18 minutes the climate turns, and the world has to begin again in its own way. It makes its own music, too: each cell sings its species' song, over a chorus of the births, kills, and deaths in view. Leave the simulation running and it keeps changing for hours.

settings.about.p1.source: A sealed biosphere of up to millions of particles, and all of them live, eat, breed, and die in your browser, simulated on the GPU with WebGPU. Some cells drink the moving light of the tide. Others graze on the photosynthesizers, and others hunt the grazers. Scavengers break down the dead and return them to the water as silt, and from that silt the next generation builds its children. Children mutate into new species. Species that bond grow into bodies: filaments, branched fronds, spirals, packed tissues. Some of these bodies grow beating tails and swim. Every 10 to 18 minutes the climate turns, and the world has to begin again in its own way. It makes its own music, too: each cell sings its species' song, over a chorus of the births, kills, and deaths in view.

gloss.silt.source: Inert grit, most of the world’s matter. It drifts on currents, every newborn cell is built out of one grain of it, and now and then life sparks from it in the light.

gloss.husk.source: A dead cell’s remains. Starved, elderly, killed and scalded cells all leave one, and eaters drop dung (smaller olive pellets). Holds leftover energy for scavengers and crumbles back into silt after about half a minute: cold water keeps carcasses for the scavengers, warm water rots them fast, and a rotting pile warms its water a little.

gloss.light.source: What plants feed on. It is dim everywhere (how dim depends on the era) and brighter inside tide bands, most of all at the height of the season. You can see it: cells, silt and stone in the bands are lit warm and bright, those outside them dim and cool, and the floor glows faintly where the light falls.

In about one era in six the water stands low and the highest ground shows as islands; the next full-water era covers them again. Each era is named for what marks it as it begins.

gloss.framboid.source: A pyrite framboid: a sphere of tiny iron sulfide crystals, a few microns across like the cells. Framboids grow where a pile of husks rots in cool water (the rot releases the sulfide), and a few lie in the mud from the start. As one oxidizes it warms its water, burning faster the warmer that water is, so a crowded, hot cluster burns itself out; spent, it crumbles to silt. Sparks of life favor their warmth, and heat-loving species gather round them. Framboids are solid like stone.

gloss.cyst.source: A dormant cell. An animal running out of energy with nothing to eat in reach may go dormant: it leaves its body, stops swimming and pulsing, grays and holds still unless jostled, leaking a little energy, and wakes at random, after about 45 seconds on average. Nothing can eat a cyst. Cysts are the seed bank that carries a lineage through hard times.

gloss.adhesion.source: How strongly cells of one species bond. Above 15%, each cell keeps up to two same-species partners with springs. Empty slots find the nearest neighbors within bond range; children start bonded to their parent if they are the same species. Bonds last until a partner dies, changes kind or stretches too far away. Bonds are the links you see and they hold bodies together. Bonded cells share the cost of living (up to 15% less upkeep), shade each other less and are armored against attack. They still pay crowding beyond their bond partners, disperse poorly and their inner cells struggle to reach silt to divide. Species without adhesion are single-celled.

gloss.adapting.source: Why the page is drawing less than it could, if it is: frames running late, the GPU busy for nearly the whole frame, the device under pressure (hot or busy, where the browser reports it), or the browser’s own pace (it hands out frames more slowly than the screen refreshes while the page has little to do: only the frame rate is lowered then). With Target fps on Auto it lowers the frame rate to 30 first, then eases what Adaptation may (work done less often, effects, the render scale), and below 30 only once nothing else is left. It climbs back after a stretch with room to spare, 60 fps last. Running fast it does not adapt.

gloss.stride.source: How much simulated time each step moves the world forward. Normally a step is 1/60 s, the most exact. When you ask for a speed the GPU can’t reach in steps that small, it takes bigger ones instead, up to 6/60 s; so does a device that can’t draw 60 frames a second, one step a frame (2/60 s at 30 fps). Bigger steps are a little coarser, but births, deaths and the variety of species stay the same over long runs.

gloss.mind.source: What this cell is doing, read from a replay of its latest decision. A cell has no brain: every frame it adds up the pulls and pushes of everything within reach (its receptors against their surface signatures, appetite for the foods its diet favors, schooling, bonds, stone), moves, then eats, divides or neither. The mode names which pull wins; hover it for the reasoning. The compass draws each pull as an arrow, its length the pull’s strength, with the cell’s heading dashed and its target as a diamond on the rim. The lamps light for conditions that shape what it does. Fleeing is an evolved aversion: no cell knows what a predator is, but lineages whose receptors happened to push them away from their hunters survived.

Flesh-eaters are drawn to animal cells, grazers (and, reluctantly, flesh-eaters) to plant cells, and husk-eaters to husks. It lets living food inside its personal space so it can reach it. A sated cell feels no appetite.

gloss.colonial.source: On average its cells attract each other. In a bonded species this packs the body tight; in a single-celled species the cells gather into swarms without ever joining.

gloss.solitary.source: On average its cells repel each other, so they spread out (or, if bonded, stretch into strands).

gloss.looseknit.source: Its cells barely attract or repel each other.

gloss.morphs.source: A single-celled species whose genome makes more than one cell type. The types never bond into a body: they are separate individuals of one species with different shapes and behaviours, like castes or life stages. Their children can be any type the developmental rule allows.

gloss.singlecelled.source: Its cells never bond: each one is a whole organism, however closely they crowd. A species bonds into multicellular bodies only once its adhesion passes 15%.

gloss.anchored.source: Barely moves and holds against the currents: a reef or a mat.

gloss.crawler.source: Moves under its own power, but too weakly to count as a swimmer, and is not simply carried by the currents. Any species that is not anchored, a swimmer or a drifter is a crawler.

gloss.focus.source: A highlight: everything outside the chosen filter is dimmed in the simulation.

gloss.links.source: Bonds between cells of one multicellular body. Single-celled species never show links.

gloss.chronicler.source: The chronicler reads the census and a ledger of who ate whom, how each species died and where it lives, and now and then writes what happened in the log: a death worth remembering and its cause, an arms race, hunters and hunted cycling, a lineage following the water, the last of a guild, what an era or an event did. It speaks only when something notable has happened, a few times an hour at most. Lab → Log → Chronicler shows its entries alone.

gloss.card.source: A species card: its portrait, sigil, song, lineage and natural history on one image, with the chronicler’s latest line about it. Save it as a PNG, and its song as a short clip. You can give the species a name of your own there.

gloss.targetfps.source: Frames per second aimed for, as a whole number of the screen’s refreshes so frames stay evenly spaced (60 on a 144 Hz screen is every second refresh, 72 fps). 30 halves the GPU’s work and saves battery; Display follows the screen’s refresh rate (120 on many phones and Macs), which costs the most. Simulated time keeps pace with real time at any rate. Auto aims for 60 and, when the device can’t keep up, drops to 30 before easing anything else, and lower (20 or 15) only once nothing else is left (shown beside Auto); it returns to 60 last, once everything else is back. A rate chosen is held even then.

guide.ecology.currents.source: Anchored photosynths thrive where currents run strong; drifting ones where they are calm. Bonded bodies live cheaply and resist attack but disperse poorly.
